title: Estate Planning Basics: Beneficiaries, TOD, Step-Up in Basis, and More
content:
Estate planning is the process of arranging how your assets will be managed and distributed when you die or become incapacitated. It's a topic many people avoid, but failing to plan can leave your loved ones with legal headaches, unnecessary taxes, and family conflict. The good news is that basic estate planning is not complicated, and even simple steps can make a profound difference.

## Why Estate Planning Matters

Without proper planning, your assets are distributed according to your state's intestacy laws, which may not reflect your wishes. Courts may become involved (probate), creating delays, public records, and legal costs. Proper estate planning ensures your assets go to the right people, as quickly and inexpensively as possible.

## Beneficiary Designations

Beneficiary designations are instructions attached directly to specific accounts that override your will. Accounts with beneficiary designations pass directly to the named beneficiaries — outside of probate. It is critical to keep these up to date, especially after major life events (marriage, divorce, birth of children, death of a beneficiary).

Accounts with beneficiary designations typically include:
- **Retirement accounts**: 401(k), IRA, Roth IRA, 403(b), pension plans
- **Life insurance policies**
- **Annuities**

**Common mistake:** Naming your estate as the beneficiary of a retirement account instead of a person. This triggers a faster required withdrawal schedule and potentially higher taxes for heirs.

**Primary vs. contingent beneficiaries:** Always name both. The contingent beneficiary receives the account if the primary beneficiary predeceases you.

## Transfer-on-Death (TOD) Accounts

TOD (or Payable-on-Death/POD for bank accounts) designations allow non-retirement brokerage and bank accounts to pass directly to named beneficiaries without going through probate. The account owner retains full control during their lifetime — the beneficiary has no rights to the account until death. TOD accounts are simple to set up and are one of the most effective probate-avoidance tools for investment assets.

## The Step-Up in Basis: A Critical Tax Concept

When you inherit an asset (stock, real estate, etc.), its cost basis is "stepped up" to the fair market value at the date of the original owner's death — not the original purchase price. This can eliminate enormous embedded capital gains.

**Example:**
- Your parent bought stock in 1990 for $10,000. By the time of their death, it's worth $200,000.
- Without step-up: If they had sold before death, they'd pay capital gains on $190,000.
- With step-up: You inherit the stock with a new cost basis of $200,000. If you sell immediately at $200,000, you owe zero capital gains tax.

This is one of the most powerful legal tax benefits in the U.S. tax code. It makes holding appreciated assets until death a potentially valuable strategy, particularly for those in high-tax situations. Note: IRAs and 401(k)s do NOT receive a step-up in basis — they are still taxed as ordinary income when withdrawn by heirs.

## Basic Estate Planning Documents

### 1. Last Will and Testament
A will specifies how your assets should be distributed and names guardians for minor children. Without a will, state law decides. Wills go through probate.

### 2. Revocable Living Trust
A trust can hold assets during your lifetime and distribute them after death — avoiding probate entirely for assets held in the trust. It also provides for incapacity. More complex to set up than a will, but highly beneficial for those with significant assets, multiple properties, or complex family situations.

### 3. Durable Power of Attorney (DPOA)
Names someone to handle financial decisions on your behalf if you become incapacitated. Without one, courts may appoint a guardian/conservator, which is costly and slow.

### 4. Healthcare Directive / Living Will
Expresses your wishes for medical treatment if you cannot communicate them, and names a healthcare proxy.

## Federal Estate Tax

The federal estate tax applies only to estates above the exemption threshold: **$13.61 million per person in 2024** ($27.22 million for married couples using portability). The top estate tax rate is 40%. Because of the high exemption, the vast majority of Americans will not owe federal estate tax. However, several states have their own estate or inheritance taxes with much lower exemption thresholds.

## Key Action Items for Everyone

1. Update beneficiary designations on all accounts and insurance policies.
2. Add TOD designations to brokerage and bank accounts.
3. Write a will if you don't have one.
4. Create a durable power of attorney and healthcare directive.
5. Consider a revocable trust if your estate is complex or above $1–2 million.
